pos: n. (the southern English county of the Weald and the Downs, where seventeen Protestants were burned at Lewes between 1555 and 1557)
etymology: Old English Sūþ Seaxe, the South Saxons, the last English kingdom to be converted.
biblical_def: Sussex is the southern county between the Downs and the sea, with the forest and iron country of the Weald behind it. It was the last of the English kingdoms to receive the Gospel, converted under Wilfrid about 681, and it was among the counties where the Marian persecution bit hardest. Between 1555 and 1557 seventeen men and women were burned in the ditch below Lewes castle, ten of them together in June 1557, the largest single burning in England outside Stratford; Richard Woodman, an ironmaster of Warbleton, was among them, and his examinations are recorded at length by Foxe. Others died at Chichester, Mayfield and East Grinstead. The county's Wealden iron trade cast the guns that armed Elizabeth's fleet. Later it was poorly served: the Downs parishes were small and the Weald remote, and the dissenting and then the evangelical interest grew slowly. The dictionary records the Lewes seventeen, and sets against the conventional reading of such deaths as the tragic cost of an intolerant age the sufferers' own reading of them, which was that a man may be killed and not harmed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a weald as a wood or open country; a stake as the post of execution; to burn as to consume with fire; constancy as firmness of mind; and to deliver as to rescue.
webster_full: WEALD, n. A wood or forest; an open country; a term found in the names of places, as the Weald of Kent.
STAKE, n. A small piece of wood sharpened and set in the ground; the post to which one condemned to burn was fastened.
BURN, v.t. To consume with fire; to reduce to ashes by the action of heat or fire.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; a standing firm; firmness of mind; stability in attachments or in principle.
DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to rescue, as from danger or destruction.
scriptures: And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Isa 43:2

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
corruption_summary: Southern county of the Downs and the Weald, last English kingdom converted, where seventeen Protestants were burned at Lewes between 1555 and 1557, ten of them on one day in June 1557.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is not the cruelty but the doctrine the cruelty enforced, and the dictionary keeps them in that order. The Lewes sufferers were examined on the sacrament and on the authority of Rome, and they died because they would not grant a corporal presence under the species nor a jurisdiction over conscience; Woodman's examinations show a Sussex ironmaster arguing both points out of the text. The strength to stand in such a place comes from a particular calculation our Lord commands, and it is a calculation about who can do what: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell” (Mat 10:28). A magistrate with a fire has less power than he supposes, and a martyr who knows this is not merely brave but correct.

The second paragraph rejects the modern framing, which treats the burnings as the regrettable product of an intolerant century on all sides and so makes the sufferers interchangeable with their judges. They were not interchangeable. The promise given to those who go through fire is given to a people and not to a position: “when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee” (Isa 43:2), which is plainly not a promise of physical immunity, since ten of them burned at Lewes in one hour. Micah supplies the register in which such a defeat is to be read, “Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me” (Mic 7:8), and the psalm gives the church's own account of its condition in this world, “for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psa 44:22). The dictionary holds that the ditch at Lewes is one of the places where English Protestantism was actually settled.

roots_lines: Greek apokteino (G615) — to kill, to put to death; “them which kill the body”, Matthew 10:28.
Greek psuche (G5590) — the soul, the life; “but are not able to kill the soul”, Matthew 10:28.
Hebrew 'esh (H784) — fire; “when thou walkest through the fire”, Isaiah 43:2.

“when I fall, I shall arise” (Mic 7:8) — the sufferers' own reading of their defeat.
“we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psa 44:22) — Richard Woodman of Warbleton.

pos: n. (the county south of London, birthplace of George Abbot, the one thoroughly Calvinist Archbishop of Canterbury)
etymology: Old English Sūþrige, the southern district or region, from sūþ, south, and -ge, a district.
biblical_def: Surrey is the county immediately south of London, running from the Thames to the Sussex border, with Guildford as its county town and Farnham Castle as a residence of the bishops of Winchester. Its chief interest in the dictionary is one man. George Abbot, born at Guildford in 1562 the son of a clothworker, rose through Balliol and the deanery of Winchester to be Archbishop of Canterbury from 1611 to 1633, and he was the only genuinely Calvinist primate the Church of England had. He worked on the Authorized Version, supported the Dutch Reformed against the Remonstrants and had English delegates sent to the Synod of Dort, opposed the Spanish match, and fought the rising Arminian party of Richard Neile and William Laud at every step; his brother Robert was bishop of Salisbury and his brother Maurice Lord Mayor of London. He was sidelined after an accident in which he killed a gamekeeper with a crossbow, and his influence was spent long before his death; Laud followed him. Abbot founded the hospital at Guildford that still bears his name. The dictionary records him as the high-water mark of Reformed doctrine in the English episcopate, and does not pretend that the office he held was thereby justified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a primate as the chief ecclesiastic; a bishop as an overseer; an archbishop as a chief bishop; humility as lowliness of mind; and a hospital as a building for the sick or the poor.
webster_full: PRIMATE, n. The chief ecclesiastic in the church; an archbishop who has jurisdiction over other bishops.
BISHOP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent; in the primitive church, the pastor of a single congregation.
ARCHBISHOP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class; a metropolitan bishop.
HUMILITY, n. In ethics, freedom from pride and arrogance; lowliness of mind; a modest estimate of one's own worth.
HOSPITAL, n. A building appropriated for the reception of sick, infirm and helpless paupers.
scriptures: A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:

Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
Jam 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
corruption_summary: County south of London and birthplace of George Abbot, Archbishop of Canterbury 1611 to 1633, the one thoroughly Calvinist English primate, who opposed the rising Arminian party and was succeeded by Laud.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the office rather than the man, and the dictionary names it even while honouring him. Abbot held the primacy of all England, a jurisdiction over other bishops with courts, revenues and a palace; the New Testament knows a bishop as the pastor of a congregation and uses the words elder, bishop and overseer interchangeably for that one office. Paul's qualifications are domestic and pastoral and assume a man known to the people he serves: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2). Titus was left to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5), a plurality in each place, not one man over a province. The dictionary therefore counts Abbot's Calvinism a mercy within a frame it still judges unwarranted.

The second paragraph gives the man his due, because the alternative reading, that a Calvinist archbishop was a contradiction in terms and his tenure of no account, is not honest either. Abbot used the office to keep Arminianism out of the English church for twenty years, to get delegates to Dort, and to resist a Spanish marriage; what followed him demonstrated what the office could do in other hands. Our Lord's rebuke to men who attend to the small and neglect “the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” (Mat 23:23) is notable for what it adds, that the lesser things ought also to have been done; a prelate who gets the doctrine right has got the weightier matter right. And the principle on which Abbot's rise and fall are both to be read is the one James states, that “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6). A clothworker's son from Guildford held the first place in the English church and ended it ignored, and the hospital he built for poor men in his own town has outlasted his court.

“and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — a plurality in each place, not one over a province.
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6) — a clothworker's son, and his hospital.

pos: n. (the southern county of Winchester and Southampton, whose bishop Stephen Gardiner was Mary's Lord Chancellor and the chief architect of the persecution)
etymology: From Southampton, Old English Hamtun, the home farm or settlement; the shire was Hamtunscir, now Hampshire.
biblical_def: Hampshire is the southern county holding the cathedral city of Winchester, ancient capital of Wessex and of England, and the port of Southampton. Its bishopric was the richest in the kingdom, and from 1531 it was held, with an interruption, by Stephen Gardiner. Gardiner was a lawyer and diplomat who had argued the king's divorce, accepted the royal supremacy and then defended the mass, transubstantiation and clerical celibacy against Cranmer in print; deprived and imprisoned under Edward, he was restored by Mary in 1553, made Lord Chancellor, and became the principal author of the policy that revived the heresy statutes and sent some three hundred people to the fire. He died in November 1555, five weeks after Ridley and Latimer burned. The county also holds Southampton, from which the Mayflower first put out in August 1620 before being driven back, and which later sent many emigrants. The dictionary names Gardiner as the clearest English case of the civil sword taken up for a doctrine, and holds the throne that frames mischief by a law to be the thing Scripture most sharply distinguishes from lawful magistracy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chancellor as a chief judicial officer; heresy as a fundamental error in religion; a statute as an act of the legislature; to recant as to retract; and boldness as courage.
webster_full: CHANCELLOR, n. A judge; the president of a court of chancery; in England, the highest judicial officer of the crown.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
STATUTE, n. An act of the legislature of a state, that extends its binding force to all the citizens.
RECANT, v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to revoke a declaration or proposition.
BOLDNESS, n. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; liberty or excessive freedom of speech.
scriptures: Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
corruption_summary: Southern county of Winchester and Southampton, whose bishop Stephen Gardiner became Mary's Lord Chancellor in 1553 and was the principal author of the revived heresy statutes.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the legal persecution of conscience, and the dictionary names the mechanism rather than merely the cruelty. Gardiner did not act as a mob; he acted as Lord Chancellor, through parliament and the courts, reviving statutes and setting commissions to work, so that every burning had a warrant. The psalmist has a name for that exact arrangement and it is the sharpest thing in Scripture on the subject: “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20). A government that legislates an injustice has not made it just; it has added the abuse of law to the original wrong, and the dictionary insists on the point because the same machinery was later turned on dissenters by Protestants.

The second paragraph states the limit of obedience, which the Hampshire sufferers found and which Scripture fixes in advance. The apostles put the question back on the court that was forbidding them to preach: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). The three in Babylon give the form of a refusal that is neither seditious nor negotiable, telling the king plainly “that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:18), and offering no resistance beyond the refusal itself. That is the pattern: no rising, no plot, no sword, and no compliance. What such men have, and what their judges generally lack, is stated by Solomon with some irony: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1). Gardiner died with the fires still burning and the policy already failing.

Hebrew 'amal (H5999) — toil, trouble, mischief; “which frameth mischief by a law”, Psalm 94:20.
Greek dikaios (G1342) — right, just, righteous; “Whether it be right in the sight of God”, Acts 4:19.
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to decide; “to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye”, Acts 4:19.
Hebrew kephir (H3715) — a young lion; “but the righteous are bold as a lion”, Proverbs 28:1.

“that we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18) — refusal without rebellion.
“the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1) — Gardiner dead in November 1555.

pos: n. (the Thames-side county of Windsor and Reading, where three men were burned in 1543 under the Act of Six Articles for the English Scriptures)
etymology: Old English Bearrucscir, probably from a Celtic wood name barroc, hilly place, with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Berkshire is the county along the upper Thames, holding Windsor, Reading and Abingdon, with the Vale of the White Horse behind it. Its sharpest episode is the Windsor burnings of 1543. The Act of Six Articles of 1539 had reimposed transubstantiation, auricular confession and clerical celibacy on pain of death, and in Windsor a faction in the royal free chapel went after the men who had been reading and discussing the English Bible in the town. Robert Testwood, a singing man of the chapel, Henry Filmer, a churchwarden, and Anthony Pearson, a priest, were convicted and burned together outside the town in July 1543; John Marbeck the organist, whose concordance of the English Bible was produced in evidence against him, was condemned and then pardoned, and his concordance, the first in English, was printed in 1550. Reading and Abingdon had great abbeys, both dissolved in 1538 and 1539, and the last abbot of Reading was hanged at his own gate. The dictionary records the Windsor three as men killed for reading, and holds the burning of a concordance to be the clearest possible confession of what their enemies were afraid of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a concordance as an index of the words of Scripture; to refine as to purify; a hammer as an instrument for driving; a furnace as a place for melting; and quick as living.
webster_full: CONCORDANCE, n. A dictionary or index in which the principal words used in the Scriptures are arranged alphabetically, with references.
REFINE, v.t. To purify; to separate from extraneous matter, as metal from dross; to clear from impurities.
HAMMER, n. An instrument for driving nails, beating metals and the like, consisting of a head and a handle.
FURNACE, n. A place where a vehement fire may be maintained, for melting ores or metals.
QUICK, a. Living; alive; not dead; speedy; done in little time; active; nimble.
scriptures: Zec 13:9

And I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried: they shall call on my name, and I will hear them: I will say, It is my people: and they shall say, The LORD is my God.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
corruption_summary: Thames-side county of Windsor and Reading, where Testwood, Filmer and Pearson were burned in July 1543 under the Six Articles, and where Marbeck's English concordance was produced in evidence against him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the Act of Six Articles itself, a Protestant king's statute reimposing Roman doctrine with death attached, and the dictionary names it as an argument against trusting reformation to a prince's conscience. The articles required belief in transubstantiation and private masses and forbade priests to marry, and men died at Windsor under them within four years of the English Bible being set up in parish churches by the same king's authority. What the prosecutors understood better than their victims is that the danger lay in the text itself; hence a concordance in evidence. Scripture describes its own operation in terms that explain the fear: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29).

The second paragraph names what the fire actually accomplishes, which is not what the men who light it intend. The furnace is Scripture's own figure for the purifying of a people, and the promise attached is a promise of relationship rather than of rescue: “I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined” (Zec 13:9). The psalmist applies the metallurgy to the words of God themselves, which are “as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6). And the reason a concordance frightened a faction in a royal chapel is given by the writer to the Hebrews, who describes the Word as alive and as penetrating past every defence: “the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit” (Heb 4:12). Marbeck was pardoned and printed his concordance seven years later, and the dictionary counts that the better record of the affair than the Act under which his friends died.

Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, to try, to prove; “and will try them as gold is tried”, Zechariah 13:9.

“as silver tried in a furnace of earth” (Psa 12:6) — the Windsor three burned in July.
“sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12) — what the Six Articles were defending against.

pos: n. (the county whose university city saw Cranmer, Ridley and Latimer tried and burned in 1555 and 1556)
etymology: From Oxford, Old English Oxnaford, the ford where oxen crossed; with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Oxfordshire is the midland county of the upper Thames, and its university city is where the English Reformation was tested in public. Cranmer, Ridley and Latimer were brought from the Tower to Oxford in 1554 to be disputed with in the Divinity School and then tried; Ridley and Latimer were burned together in the ditch outside Balliol in October 1555, Latimer bidding Ridley play the man, and Cranmer, after signing a series of recantations in prison, was brought to St Mary's in March 1556 to read a final submission, repudiated it from the pulpit instead, and put the hand that had signed into the fire first. The university itself was divided for a century afterward and became in the sixteen-twenties and thirties the centre of the Arminian and Laudian reaction; Laud was its chancellor. John Wycliffe had been a fellow of Balliol and master of Balliol two centuries earlier, and the Lollard movement began in the Oxford schools. The dictionary records the three deaths and marks that it was a recanting man's public retraction of his own recantation that did the most for the Protestant cause in England.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a recantation as the retracting of a former declaration; a disputation as a formal debate; the gospel as the glad tidings of salvation; to prosper as to succeed; and inspiration as the supernatural influence of the Spirit.
webster_full: RECANTATION, n. The act of recanting; a declaration that contradicts a former one; retraction.
DISPUTATION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition; a public debate in the schools.
GOSPEL, n. The history of the birth, life, actions, death, resurrection, ascension and doctrine of Jesus Christ.
PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed; to be fortunate or successful in any undertaking.
INSPIRATION, n. The supernatural influence of the Spirit of God on the human mind, by which prophets and apostles were qualified to deliver truth.
scriptures: Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Midland county whose university city saw Cranmer, Ridley and Latimer tried and burned in 1555 and 1556, and which later became the centre of the Laudian reaction under Laud's chancellorship.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of a university's machinery to procure a recantation, and the dictionary names it as the particular temptation of learned men. Cranmer was not simply condemned; he was argued with, isolated, worn down and offered his life, and he signed six times. That is a more effective instrument than a stake, and it nearly worked. What broke it was not a better disputation but a man's return to the only standard that settles such questions, and Isaiah states the standard in the form of a test any hearer may apply: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). A doctor of divinity who grants that rule has no way of keeping a recantation he knows to be false.

The second paragraph states the ground of confidence, which belongs to the Word and not to the men who hold it. Cranmer failed repeatedly and the cause did not; Oxford itself went the other way within two generations and the cause did not fail then either. The reason is that the instrument has its own guarantee: “So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). Its origin is not human in the first place, for “the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21). And the right posture toward it under pressure is Paul's, stated as a refusal to be embarrassed: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Rom 1:16). Cranmer was ashamed for a season in a prison and was not ashamed at St Mary's, and the dictionary records the second occasion as the one that counted.

Greek epaischunomai (G1870) — to be ashamed of; “For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ”, Romans 1:16.
Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — emptily, in vain, void; “it shall not return unto me void”, Isaiah 55:11.
Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to advance, to prosper, to succeed; “it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it”, Isaiah 55:11.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, to carry, to be moved; “spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost”, 2 Peter 1:21.

“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — Oxford turning Laudian within two generations.
“I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ” (Rom 1:16) — Cranmer at St Mary's, March 1556.

pos: n. (the Chiltern county whose Lollard communities around Amersham were repeatedly detected and abjured between 1462 and 1522)
etymology: From Buckingham, Old English Buccingahamm, the river meadow of Bucca's people; with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Buckinghamshire runs from the Thames at Marlow over the Chiltern hills to the Ouse, and the Chiltern parishes held the most persistent Lollard community in England. From the fourteen-sixties to the fifteen-twenties the bishops of Lincoln detected, examined and abjured groups of men and women around Amersham, Chesham, Great Marlow and Hughenden who read and lent English books, denied purgatory and the corporal presence, and taught each other the Commandments, the Creed and the Epistles in English. The abjurations of 1464 and 1506 were followed by the great sweep of 1511, when sixty or more were examined, several relapsed persons were burned and many were made to carry faggots and wear badges; another detection followed in 1521 and 1522. These were not scholars. They were husbandmen, wheelwrights and their wives, and what they possessed was a few quires of a translated Gospel or Epistle passed from house to house and learned by heart. The dictionary records the Chiltern Lollards as the proof that a people will teach itself the Scriptures if it is given them and will go on doing it under penalty for sixty years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to abjure as to renounce upon oath; a faggot as a bundle of sticks; to catechise as to instruct by question; a testimony as a solemn declaration; and to perish as to be destroyed.
webster_full: ABJURE, v.t. To renounce upon oath; to abandon; to retract, recant or recall a declaration upon oath.
FAGGOT, n. A bundle of sticks, twigs or small branches of trees, used for fuel; a bundle borne as a penance.
CATECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers; to instruct in the principles of religion.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation; in Scripture, the two tables of the law; the word of God.
PERISH, v.i. To die; to lose life in any manner; to be destroyed; to come to nothing.
scriptures: Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.
And all thy children shall be taught of the LORD; and great shall be the peace of thy children.
Act 9:31
Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied.
corruption_summary: Chiltern county whose Lollard communities around Amersham and Chesham were detected and abjured repeatedly between 1462 and 1522, several relapsed persons being burned in the sweep of 1511.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Scriptures are competent to teach the unlearned without an intermediary, and the Chilterns are the English evidence. Wheelwrights and their wives, with a few quires of translated Gospel between a dozen households, held the Commandments, the Creed and the substance of the Epistles in memory and taught their children; they were examined by bishops' officers who were better educated than they were and were not shaken. The psalmist claims exactly this effect for the text, that “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7). Simple is not a slight; it is the category God undertakes to teach.

The second thing to recover is the cost and the pattern of a church that lives on so little. The sweep of 1511 burned the relapsed and sent the rest home carrying faggots and wearing badges, and the community re-formed and was detected again ten years later. Solomon's warning names what such a people had and their persecutors lacked: “Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he” (Pro 29:18). The promise they were living on is Isaiah's, that “all thy children shall be taught of the LORD; and great shall be the peace of thy children” (Isa 54:13), which is a promise of direct instruction and was being fulfilled in Chiltern kitchens. And the ordinary result of such teaching, when the persecution lifts, is the one Luke records: “Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied” (Act 9:31). When Tyndale's New Testament reached these valleys in 1526 it did not find them unprepared.

pos: n. (the Kentish Weald town that was a centre of Lollard belief, and whose steeple gave English a proverb about false reasoning)
etymology: Old English Tenet wara denn, the swine pasture of the men of Thanet, the Weald woodland having been held by the men of that island.
biblical_def: Tenterden is the small town on the edge of the Kentish Weald, a limb of the Cinque Ports when the Rother was still navigable, and one of the places where Lollard belief ran strongest and longest in the south-east. The Kentish detections of 1511 and 1512 under Archbishop Warham examined scores of people from Tenterden, Cranbrook, Benenden and Rolvenden; William Carder of Tenterden, a weaver, was burned, as were Agnes Grebill of Tenterden and others, and many more abjured. What they were accused of holding is consistent across the depositions: that the sacrament remains bread, that images ought not to be worshipped, that pilgrimage is waste, and that the Gospel should be had in English. The town also gave English a proverb. Bishop Hugh Latimer retold in a sermon the tale of a commission enquiring why Sandwich haven had silted, at which an old man answered that it was the building of Tenterden steeple, and the phrase became the standing English name for a cause confidently assigned and plainly false. The dictionary keeps both the martyrs and the proverb, and holds that the second is a useful warning to men confident of their own reasoning in religion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a deposition as testimony on oath; to abjure as to renounce on oath; a haven as a harbour; inference as a conclusion drawn; and sophistry as fallacious reasoning.
webster_full: DEPOSITION, n. The act of giving testimony under oath; the attested written testimony of a witness.
ABJURE, v.t. To renounce upon oath; to retract, recant or recall a declaration upon oath.
HAVEN, n. A harbour; a port; a bay or inlet of the sea where ships can ride in safety.
INFERENCE, n. A truth or proposition drawn from another which is admitted or supposed to be true; a conclusion.
SOPHISTRY, n. Fallacious reasoning; reasoning sound in appearance only.
scriptures: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Heb 12:4
Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.
corruption_summary: Kentish Weald town and Lollard centre whose weaver William Carder and Agnes Grebill were burned after the Kentish detections of 1511, and whose steeple gave English a proverb for false reasoning.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the abjuration, the formal oath of renunciation which the courts preferred to a burning because it cost nothing and broke more people. Most of those detected in the Kentish sweeps of 1511 and 1512 abjured; a few would not, and Carder the weaver and Agnes Grebill were burned. The dictionary names abjuration as the instrument that did the real damage, because a community that has sworn away its confession in a bishop's court has to be rebuilt from nothing. What the few who refused demonstrated is that the prosecution cannot reach the thing it is after: “I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). The method such men are commanded is openness, not prudent silence, for “what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops” (Mat 10:27).

The second paragraph takes up the proverb, because the dictionary judges it useful rather than merely quaint. Tenterden steeple is the English name for a cause asserted with total confidence and no relation to its effect, and religion is where men do this most. The Lollards were charged with error by a hierarchy entirely sure of its reasoning about the sacrament; the hierarchy was wrong. That is not an argument for suspending judgment, since Scripture never commends that, but for locating the test outside oneself. And the victory the sufferers claimed is located outside themselves too: “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). Those who abjured are not written off here. The writer to the Hebrews addresses people who had not yet been pressed to the limit, reminding them “Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin” (Heb 12:4), which is a word to the comfortable and not a sneer at the broken.

pos: n. (the Kentish Weald clothing town, a Lollard and then a Puritan centre, from which Wealden broadcloth and Wealden preaching both went out)
etymology: Old English cran broc, the brook of the cranes, from cran, a crane, and broc, a brook.
biblical_def: Cranbrook is the chief of the Kentish Weald cloth towns, and its great perpendicular church was built out of broadcloth money in the fifteenth century. It appears repeatedly in the Kentish Lollard detections of 1511 and 1512 alongside Tenterden and Benenden, and under Mary it furnished martyrs; it then became one of the most thoroughly Puritan parishes in the county, with a succession of preaching ministers and a strong body of substantial clothiers to maintain them. Richard Fletcher was vicar in the middle of Elizabeth's reign, and the parish kept lectures and exercises going through the next century; Weald families from Cranbrook and its neighbours emigrated to New England in numbers, and the Kentish names are scattered through the Massachusetts and Connecticut records. The cloth trade declined in the seventeenth century when the new draperies took the market, and the town shrank to a village with a cathedral-sized church. The dictionary records Cranbrook as a place from which something went out in both centuries, cloth to Europe and men with the Gospel to the parishes and across the Atlantic, and takes the occasion to state what a sending church is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to publish as to make known; a company as an assemblage; to sound as to make a noise; broadcloth as a fine woollen cloth; and a creature as a created being.
webster_full: PUBLISH, v.t. To discover or make known to mankind or to people in general what before was private or unknown.
COMPANY, n. An assemblage of persons; a number of persons united for the same purpose, or in a joint concern.
SOUND, v.i. To make a noise; to utter a voice; to be conveyed in sound; to be spread or published.
BROADCLOTH, n. A species of woollen cloth, so called from its breadth.
CREATURE, n. That which is created; every being besides the Creator; a human being.
scriptures: Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
For from you sounded out the word of the Lord not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith to God-ward is spread abroad; so that we need not to speak any thing.
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
corruption_summary: Chief Kentish Weald cloth town, named in the Lollard detections of 1511 and later among the most Puritan parishes in Kent, which sent broadcloth to Europe and emigrants to New England.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a congregation is a place things leave from rather than a place things are kept in, and that this is true whether the thing leaving is a bale of cloth or a family with a Bible. Cranbrook was built by export. Its church was paid for by broadcloth sold in Antwerp, and in the following century the same households paid for lectures and then supplied emigrants to Massachusetts. Scripture's standing example of unplanned dispersal doing the work of a mission is the persecution at Jerusalem, where “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4); a scattering is not necessarily a loss.

The second thing to recover is that the sending church is itself a testimony, so that the going out does the work of argument. Paul tells the Thessalonians that he no longer needs to make their case, since “from you sounded out the word of the Lord not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith to God-ward is spread abroad” (1Th 1:8). The psalmist makes the publishing a company rather than an individual feat: “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11). The commission is universal in scope and leaves no congregation exempt from being a point of departure, “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). Cranbrook shrank to a village and kept its enormous church, and the dictionary reads that as a fair emblem: the building was the smaller half of what the trade bought, and what went out of the town outlasted what stayed in it.

pos: n. (the Buckinghamshire lace town where John Newton was curate and where he and William Cowper produced the Olney Hymns of 1779)
etymology: Old English Ollaneg, Olla's island or water-meadow, from a personal name and eg, an island.
biblical_def: Olney is the small lace-making town on the Ouse in north Buckinghamshire, and it is one of the few English villages whose name belongs to the history of worship. John Newton, who had been master of a slave ship and was converted at sea and then over years of reading, was ordained in 1764 and came to Olney as curate, where he stayed sixteen years. He preached to lacemakers and labourers, kept a weekly meeting for children, and wrote a hymn for most of his prayer meetings so that the congregation might sing what had just been preached. William Cowper, the poet, came to live in the town in 1767 and became Newton's friend and collaborator despite the recurring derangement that overshadowed his life. Their joint collection, the Olney Hymns, was published in 1779 with three hundred and forty-eight pieces, Newton writing the greater number, including the hymn beginning Amazing grace, and Cowper contributing sixty-eight, among them God moves in a mysterious way and There is a fountain filled with blood. The dictionary records the book as the plainest English demonstration that doctrine put into verse and sung by a congregation will outlive the sermons it came from.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hymn as a song of adoration to God; grace as the free unmerited favour of God; a fountain as a spring; to guide as to lead; and to shine as to emit light.
webster_full: HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God; among pagans, a poem in honour of a deity; a sacred lyric.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favour of God; the divine influence which renews the heart and restrains from sin.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; the source or first principle of anything.
GUIDE, v.t. To lead or direct in a way; to conduct in a course or path; to influence or direct.
SHINE, v.i. To emit rays of light; to give light; to be bright; to be lively or animated.
scriptures: Mal 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
Pro 4:18
But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
Luk 1:79
To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.

To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.
corruption_summary: Buckinghamshire lace town where John Newton was curate for sixteen years from 1764 and where he and William Cowper produced the Olney Hymns of 1779, three hundred and forty-eight pieces in all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a hymn is a vehicle for doctrine and is answerable to doctrine, not a vehicle for feeling that happens to use religious words. Newton wrote for a particular prayer meeting on a particular text so that his lacemakers would carry the week's teaching home in a form they could not easily lose; the hymns are therefore full of the substance of the faith, ruin, grace, imputation, perseverance, and they name it. The figure Newton reached for most often is the one Scripture itself uses for the arrival of mercy on a blind man, and the apostolic commission states it as the purpose of preaching: “To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18).

The second thing to recover is Cowper, and here the dictionary speaks against a sentimentality that would smooth him out. Cowper believed for long stretches that he himself was lost, attempted his own life, and wrote some of the best hymns in the language out of that darkness; his collaborator was a converted slaver who never stopped calling himself a wretch. Neither man is evidence that assurance is easy, and the hymns are not cheerful. What they hold to is a dawn promised rather than felt: “unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings” (Mal 4:2), and a path that brightens by degrees rather than at once, since “the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18). Zacharias had sung the same thing of men still sitting in the dark, that God would “give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luk 1:79). Olney produced that book out of a curacy among lacemakers, and the dictionary counts it among the most fruitful sixteen years any English parish ever had.

pos: n. (the Berkshire town whose great abbey was dissolved in 1538 and whose townsmen then rebuilt its civic and charitable life for themselves)
etymology: Old English Abbandun, Abba's hill; the monastery took its name from the hill and gave it to the town.
biblical_def: Abingdon is the Thames-side town below Oxford, and until 1538 it was essentially the property of its abbey. The Benedictine house, refounded in the tenth century, was one of the richest in England, holding the manor, the market, the mills and the bridge tolls, and the townsmen had rioted against it more than once over their want of a parish church of their own and over the abbot's control of trade. At the Dissolution the house was surrendered and almost entirely demolished for its stone, so that very little of it now stands. What followed is the part the dictionary records. The town obtained a charter in 1556, became the county town of Berkshire, refounded its school as Roysse's in 1563 out of a merchant's bequest, maintained Christ's Hospital with its almshouses from an older guild endowment, and built the county hall in the sixteen-seventies. Its dissenting congregations, Baptist and Presbyterian, were vigorous from the Restoration onward. The dictionary records Abingdon as a case of a town taking up, for itself and badly at first, the schooling and the relief of the poor that an abbey had done for it, and holds that this was the right direction of travel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an almshouse as a house for the poor; a charter as a written instrument of privileges; a breach as a gap; to repair as to restore; and reproach as censure or shame.
webster_full: ALMSHOUSE, n. A house appropriated for the use of the poor; a house maintained by charity.
CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or privilege.
BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap or opening made by breaking; the violation of a law or covenant.
REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, waste or injury; to mend; to rebuild.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; scorn; the cause of shame or disgrace.
scriptures: Neh 1:3

And they said unto me, The remnant that are left of the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach: the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire.
Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Neh 6:3
And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?
Dan 9:19
O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for thine own sake, O my God: for thy city and thy people are called by thy name.
corruption_summary: Thames-side Berkshire town owned by its Benedictine abbey until 1538, demolished for its stone, after which the townsmen obtained a charter, refounded their school and maintained their own almshouses.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the monastic lordship of a town, and the dictionary names it as the real grievance the Abingdon rioters had long before any reformer reached them. The abbey held the market, the mills, the bridge tolls and the right of presentation, and would not let the townsmen have a parish church they could call theirs; relief of the poor and schooling came as the abbot's charity rather than as the town's duty. A religious house that owns a town does both of them harm. When it went, the townsmen were left with Nehemiah's situation and had to make Nehemiah's answer: the report was that “the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire” (Neh 1:3), and the response was not a lament but a proposal, “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17).

The second paragraph names what the dictionary thinks the right direction of travel was, and it is not nostalgia for the abbey. A charter in 1556, a school refounded out of a merchant's bequest in 1563, almshouses kept out of a guild endowment, a county hall in the sixteen-seventies and strong Baptist and Presbyterian congregations by the end of the century: that is a town doing for itself, under God, what had been done for it. The work is slow and gets interrupted, and the proper reply to those who would call a man down from it is Nehemiah's: “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down” (Neh 6:3). The dictionary adds the prayer that belongs with such rebuilding, which is a prayer about God's name and not the town's credit: “O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for thine own sake, O my God” (Dan 9:19). An abbey reduced to a gateway and a town that learned to keep its own poor is, on balance, a gain.
